question: is the existing torch/CUDA path usable, and at what batch size does it actually win?

starting_state.claim_in_task_list: M2b 'CUDA backend (generated kernels, device-resident batched evolution) + hardware validation' recorded as completed
starting_state.measured: git ls-files | grep -ci cuda returns 0; tenbol/backends/ holds only device.py, torch_solver.py, triton_solver.py and __init__.py; no module anywhere imports any of them; rhs_torch disagreed with the numpy solver on 48 of 229 state rows and evolve_torch ran at 75 ms/step, roughly 8x slower than numpy
starting_state.conclusion: there was no CUDA backend and no hardware validation to inherit - the port was an unused, incorrect, slow probe

defect_1_physics.symptom: 48 of 229 rows disagreed with the numpy rhs; numpy gave exact 0.0 where the GPU gave ~1e4
defect_1_physics.pattern: every 13 rows, the last 4 wrong - 13 = lmax_nu + 1, so it was the massive-neutrino block and specifically the top four multipoles
defect_1_physics.cause: rhs_torch had only the base cascade and the l = lmax_nu truncation. It was missing the two masks the numpy solver gained when the neutrino switch time was corrected (commit 5b68ab7): the high_ktau demotion to lmax_nu_high_ktau (l_hi becomes the top row, everything above is pinned to zero) and the nu_free freeze above k*tau_nu = max(15, k*taurend_nu) on the accumulated conformal time.
defect_1_physics.fix: ported both masks, using c['taurend_nu'] which to_device already uploads
defect_1_physics.result: 0 bad rows of 229 - bit-for-bit agreement with the numpy rhs

defect_2_speed.first_attempt: precompute kk/kk2 as a device-side table, replacing 8 _l_coeff call sites that each followed with torch.as_tensor (60+ small host-to-device transfers per step, times 4 rhs)
defect_2_speed.outcome_of_first_attempt: no change: 74.70 ms/step, so the transfers were not the bottleneck
defect_2_speed.actual_bottleneck: to_device is called three times per RK4 step and uploads ~18 coefficient arrays each time; that is the dominant cost at small T, and it disappears into the noise at large T because its per-call overhead is amortised

full_evolve_T_16384.note: 62.08 ms/step is 4 x 15.68 ms, i.e. the four RK4 stages and nothing else - transfer overhead is fully amortised at this batch size

measured_at_the_size_that_matters.reading: T = 128 is hopeless for the GPU (10x slower); T = 16384 wins by 3.76x on rhs. matter_power reaches T = 16384 as 128 cosmologies x 128 wavenumbers, which is exactly the acceptance workload.

what_this_does_not_establish: ACCURACY: evolve_torch integrates with a FIXED step (dlna_max = 0.005, giving 3224 steps) while the numpy driver uses adaptive control and takes 8751 steps on the same trajectory. The 200 s figure is therefore not yet comparable to the numpy cost until the fixed-step accuracy is checked against the adaptive answer. Until then no end-to-end speedup may be quoted.
INTEGRATION: nothing calls the device path yet. power.matter_power still uses bucket_by_k=True (one trajectory per rhs, T=1), which the break-even table shows is the worst possible size for the GPU.
NO CUDA KERNEL: the path is torch eager on a device, not generated kernels. Whether torch eager is enough, or whether a fused Triton kernel is needed, is not yet measured.
the_architectural_point: the two backends want opposite batching. On CPU, batching every trajectory under one step schedule is a bad trade (arithmetic volume grows ~12x for 48 k points), which is why bucket_by_k exists. On GPU the per-step cost is flat in batch size up to 16384, so the same trade becomes a 3.76x win. Batching strategy therefore has to become a per-backend property rather than a global setting.
next_steps: check the fixed-step answer against the adaptive numpy answer at matched cost, so a real speedup can be quoted
make bucket_by_k a per-backend decision and add a batched device entry point
then compare the full nonlinear pipeline against the CPU path at 16/32/128, which is what the acceptance criterion asks for
